topics.deep:
- **Relational model** (E. F. Codd, 1970, IBM): data in **relations (tables)**. Formal vs informal terms: **relation = table, tuple = row/record, attribute = column/field, domain = set of permitted atomic values, degree = number of attributes (columns), cardinality = number of tuples (rows)**, relation schema = name + attributes, relation instance = current tuples. Formally a relation is a **subset of the Cartesian product** D1 x D2 x ... x Dn of its domains. Properties: no duplicate tuples, tuple order and attribute order irrelevant, values atomic (1NF), each attribute has unique name. Do not confuse *column cardinality* (distinct values; low cardinality = many repeated values) with relation cardinality (row count).
- **Attribute value scales:** nominal (no order), **ordinal** (ranked, spacing unmeasured - low/medium/high), interval, ratio.
- **Keys:** **Super key** - any set of attributes that uniquely identifies tuples (need not be minimal). **Candidate key** - minimal super key (no proper subset is a super key). **Primary key** - the chosen candidate key, not null. **Alternate key** - candidate keys not chosen as primary. **Composite key** - key with more than one attribute. **Foreign key** - attribute(s) referencing the primary/candidate key of the same or another relation; may be NULL (unless constrained) and may repeat; a table can have several foreign keys. **Surrogate key** - system generated. Every candidate key is a super key, not vice versa; number of super keys of R(A,B,C) with sole key A = 4.
- **Integrity constraints:** **Domain constraint** (values from attribute domain, datatype), **Key constraint** (key values unique), **Entity integrity** (primary key cannot be NULL), **Referential integrity** (FK value must match a PK value in referenced relation or be null; enforced between two relations). Referential actions on delete/update: CASCADE, SET NULL, SET DEFAULT, RESTRICT/NO ACTION. Others: not null, check, semantic/business rules, triggers, assertions.
- **Codd's 12 rules** (numbered 0 to 12 = thirteen, conventionally 'twelve rules'): information rule, guaranteed access, systematic null treatment, active online catalog, comprehensive data sublanguage, view updating, high-level insert/update/delete, physical and logical data independence, integrity independence, distribution independence, non-subversion rule.
- **Query languages:** **procedural** (relational algebra - how to get) vs **non-procedural / declarative** (relational calculus, SQL - what to get). Tuple relational calculus (TRC) and domain relational calculus (DRC; QBE). Relational algebra and safe calculus are equally expressive (relationally complete).
- **Relational algebra operators:**
| Operator | Symbol | Kind | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Selection | sigma | unary | filters rows by predicate |
| Projection | pi | unary | picks columns, removes duplicates |
| Rename | rho | unary | renames relation/attributes |
| Union | U | binary | union-compatible relations |
| Intersection | n | binary | derived: R n S = R - (R - S) |
| Set difference | - | binary | R - S = tuples in R not in S |
| Cartesian product | X | binary | degree adds, cardinality multiplies |
| Natural join | join | binary | equi-join on common attributes, duplicate column dropped |
| Theta/equi join | join(theta) | binary | condition-based |
| Division | / | binary | 'for all' queries |
| Outer joins | left/right/full | binary | keep unmatched with NULL |
Fundamental (basic) operators: select, project, union, difference, Cartesian product, rename. Join, intersection, division are derived. **Aggregate/grouping** operator is an extension. Examples: sigma Marks>80 (STUDENT); pi Name,Marks (STUDENT); sigma Gender='F' AND Marks>60 (STUDENT).
- **Cardinality and degree rules:** Cartesian R X S -> degree = dR + dS, cardinality = nR x nS. Union cardinality <= nR + nS. Intersection <= min. Selection cardinality <= n; projection cardinality <= n (duplicates removed). Natural join cardinality between 0 and nR x nS. Division result attributes = attributes(R) - attributes(S).
- **Worked example:** R(A,B) = {(1,x),(2,y)}, S(A,B) = {(2,y),(3,z)}. R U S = 3 tuples; R n S = {(2,y)}; R - S = {(1,x)}; S - R = {(3,z)}; R X S has 4 tuples and 4 attributes.
- **Views and relations:** a *base relation* is stored; a *derived relation / view* is computed. Null means unknown, inapplicable or withheld; NULL <> 0 and NULL <> blank.
- **Typical traps:** 'Which is unary?' - select, project, rename. 'Which is NOT a relational algebra operator?' - GROUP BY/ORDER BY/LIKE are SQL, not core algebra; 'cross join' is just product. Order symbol-name match: pi projection, sigma selection, X product, rho rename, bowtie join. Degree != cardinality. Primary key cannot be NULL; foreign key can. Super key needs no minimality. Candidate key minimal. Domain of an attribute = permitted values.
- **Likely question angles:** (1) Cardinality/degree after Cartesian product of two given relations. (2) Express 'students with marks above 80' in algebra. (3) Which operator needs union compatibility? (4) Derived vs fundamental operators. (5) Which Codd rule is about NULLs or views? (6) Count super keys given candidate keys. (7) Referential integrity on delete cascade outcome. (8) Procedural vs declarative language examples. (9) Can a foreign key be null / duplicate? (10) Result of division. (11) Natural join vs equi-join column count.

topics.title: 4. SQL — DDL, DML, Queries, Joins, Functions
topics.theory:
- **SQL = Structured Query Language** (the database language). **Categories:** **DDL** (CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME) · **DML** (SELECT, **INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE**) · **DCL** (GRANT, REVOKE) · **TCL** (COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT).
- **DROP TABLE** deletes table and structure permanently; **DELETE** removes rows (WHERE; one or many; rollback-able); **TRUNCATE** removes all rows, keeps structure, DDL (may not be rolled back in some DBs); **ALTER TABLE** adds/drops/modifies columns.
- **SELECT syntax:** `SELECT [DISTINCT] cols FROM table [WHERE cond] [GROUP BY] [HAVING] [ORDER BY col ASC|DESC]` — **only SELECT and FROM are mandatory**. `*` = all columns; **DISTINCT** = unique values.
- **Operators:** comparison `=, <>, !=, >, <, >=, <=`; `LIKE` pattern match with wildcards **`%` (zero/one/many chars)** and `_` (one char); `IN`, `BETWEEN a AND b` (inclusive), `IS NULL` (not = NULL); **`||` concatenation** (Oracle); comments `-- single line`, `/* … */`.
- **Aggregate functions:** COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX (not cross product, union, intersect, minus — those are set operators). `GROUP BY` groups rows with same values; HAVING filters groups.
- **Joins:** INNER (matching in both), **LEFT OUTER (all left + matched right)**, RIGHT OUTER, **FULL OUTER (all records when match in either)**, **SELF join = table joined to itself**, CROSS join.
- **Views:** virtual table derived from base tables/other views; can be queried like a table; updatable only under restrictions. `DROP SCHEMA … RESTRICT` drops only if schema is empty; CASCADE drops everything.
- **Functions:** ROUND, **CEILING (smallest integer ≥ x)**, FLOOR, DATEDIFF, GETDATE/SYSDATE (SYSDATETIME = date-time **without** time-zone offset), TRIM, **CASE/DECODE** (return value matching an expression), single-row functions. **Datatypes:** INT, REAL, FLOAT, CHAR, VARCHAR, DATE, TIME, TIMESTAMP, INTERVAL ("BASE" is not one).
- **Second-highest value:** `SELECT MAX(result) FROM student WHERE result < (SELECT MAX(result) FROM student)`.

qs.stem: Which of the following languages is referred to as a database language?
qs.sol: Structured Query Language : SQL is the standard language used to define, manipulate, and retrieve data from databases.
qs.rel: SQL is the standard database language (DDL + DML + DCL + TCL). Neighbours: QBE, PL/SQL (procedural extension), relational algebra is theoretical, embedded SQL in host languages.

qs.stem: What is the full-form of SQL?
qs.sol: The full form of SQL is Structured Query Language.
qs.rel: SQL = Structured Query Language, originally SEQUEL at IBM; ANSI/ISO standard. Neighbours: SQL is declarative, not case-sensitive for keywords, expansions of DDL/DML/DCL/TCL.

qs.stem: Which of the following is NOT an aggregate function in SQL?
qs.sol: COUNT, SUM, and MAXIMUM/MAX are aggregate-style functions. CROSS PRODUCT is a relational operation, not an aggregate function.
qs.rel: Aggregate functions: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX. Not aggregates: CROSS PRODUCT, UPPER, ROUND (single-row). Neighbours: ignore NULLs except COUNT(*), used with GROUP BY and HAVING.

qs.stem: Which of the following is a Comparison operator in Structured Query Language?
qs.sol:
In SQL, comparison operators are used to compare two values and return a boolean result (true or false). The operator '>=' checks if the left value is greater than or equal to the right value. It is a valid comparison operator because it evaluates a condition and returns a logical outcome.
 On the other hand, operators like '+' (addition), '*' (multiplication), and '/' (division) are arithmetic operators. They perform mathematical operations and do not evaluate conditions. Therefore, they are not comparison operators.
qs.rel: Comparison operators: =, <>, <, >, <=, >=, plus BETWEEN, IN, LIKE, IS NULL. Contrast with logical (AND, OR, NOT), arithmetic, concatenation (||) and set operators (UNION).

qs.stem: Which of the following command is used with SQL SELECT statement to return only distinct (different) values?
qs.sol:
Modified from the official paper: the printed question asks about Oracle, where both “UNIQUE” and “DISTINCT” return distinct rows; it is asked here for SQL, where only “DISTINCT” does. DSSSB’s key marked “UNIQUE”, and DSSSB then ignored this question for all candidates.

In SQL, SELECT DISTINCT returns only distinct rows. “UNIQUE” is not a SELECT keyword in standard SQL (in a SELECT list it is an Oracle-only synonym), and “DIFFERENT” and “SINGLE” are not SQL keywords.
qs.rel: DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the result set (Oracle also accepts UNIQUE). Neighbours: DISTINCT applies to all selected columns, COUNT(DISTINCT col), UNION removes duplicates but UNION ALL keeps them.

qs.stem: Which of the following keyword is used in Oracle SQL to sort the result-set in ascending or descending order?
qs.sol: The correct keyword is ORDER BY. This clause sorts the result-set in ascending or descending order based on specified columns.
qs.rel: ORDER BY sorts results, ASC default, DESC optional, multiple columns allowed, always last clause. Neighbours: GROUP BY groups rows, ordering by column position or alias, NULL ordering.

qs.stem: What does the DROP TABLE command do?

opts.A: Deletes a table permanently from the database
opts.B: Deletes all records in a table but keeps the structure
opts.C: Deletes only duplicate rows in a table
opts.D: Restores deleted data from the table

qs.sol: DROP TABLE removes the table object, including its stored definition and records. A later query cannot use that table name unless the table is created again.
qs.rel: DROP TABLE deletes structure and data permanently (DDL, auto-commit). Contrast: TRUNCATE (rows only, keeps structure), DELETE (rows, DML, rollbackable). Dependent views and constraints are affected.

qs.stem: Which of the following is an Aggregate operator in Structured Query Language (SQL)?
qs.sol: Count, Min, Max, Avg, Sum all are aggregate functions in SQL
qs.rel: Aggregate operators: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX. Neighbours: aggregates ignore NULL (except COUNT(*)), cannot appear in WHERE, need HAVING for group filter.

qs.stem:
Which of the following represents the "inner" join operation?

A
B
C
D
qs.sol: An inner join returns only rows that have matching values in both tables. This operation corresponds to the intersection of the two sets in a Venn diagram, highlighting only the overlapping region.
qs.rel: Inner join returns only matching rows. Contrast: left/right outer (keep unmatched side with NULLs), full outer, cross (product), natural (common columns), self join. Venn-diagram question style.

qs.stem: Which of the following statement is a part of Data Manipulative Language in Structured Query Language?
qs.sol:
DML changes rows in a table; DELETE removes selected rows.

ALTER TABLE is DDL, while COPY and PASTE are not the intended standard DML statements.
qs.rel: DML commands: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE. ALTER, CREATE, DROP, TRUNCATE are DDL; GRANT/REVOKE DCL; COMMIT/ROLLBACK TCL. Common trap: TRUNCATE is DDL despite deleting rows.

qs.stem: Which of the following operator of SQL is used in WHERE clause for match a character pattern in database?
qs.sol: In SQL, the LIKE operator is used in the WHERE clause to match character patterns.
qs.note: Table/figure from the original paper was not captured. Use the explanation to see the correct matching.
qs.rel: LIKE matches patterns using % (any number of characters) and _ (single character). Neighbours: NOT LIKE, ESCAPE clause, IN, BETWEEN, case sensitivity differs by DBMS, REGEXP.

qs.stem: Which of the following is NOT a part of Data Definitions Language in Relational Database Management System?
qs.sol: Insert table
qs.rel: DDL commands: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME. INSERT is DML. Neighbours: DDL statements auto-commit in Oracle; DCL = GRANT/REVOKE; TCL = COMMIT/ROLLBACK/SAVEPOINT.

qs.stem: The SQL ALTER TABLE statement is used to:

opts.A: Add, delete, or modify columns in an existing table
opts.B: Drop an existing table in a database
opts.C: Insert or modify records in a table
opts.D: Delete existing records in a table

qs.sol: The SQL ALTER TABLE command is used to modify the structure of an existing database table. It allows users to add, delete, or modify columns within that specific table schema without affecting the data itself. Other commands like DROP TABLE remove the entire table, while INSERT and UPDATE handle data manipulation rather than structural changes.
qs.rel: ALTER TABLE changes structure: ADD, MODIFY, DROP COLUMN, rename, add constraint. Contrast with UPDATE (changes data) and DROP TABLE. Dropping a column is allowed with DROP COLUMN.

qs.stem: Which of the following SQL joint statements returns all the records from the left table and the matched records from the right table?
qs.sol:
A join combines rows from two tables according to a matching condition. An inner join keeps matching pairs; an outer join also preserves unmatched rows from its designated side, supplying NULL for the missing partner.

The preserved side determines which rows survive when no partner satisfies the join condition. A matched row contributes values from both tables; NULL marks an absent partner, rather than an absent preserved row.

Take left-table identifiers {1, 2} and right-table identifiers {2, 3}, and join on equal identifiers. The matching pair has identifier 2.

Preserve the left-table identifier 1 even though no right-table row matches it. Its right-table columns receive NULL. …
qs.rel: LEFT OUTER JOIN keeps all left rows plus matches, NULL for unmatched right. Contrast: RIGHT, FULL (both sides), INNER; result count of left join >= left table rows.

qs.stem: Which of the following operator is used as concatenation operator in SQL?
qs.sol: In standard SQL, the double vertical bar operator || is used for string concatenation.
qs.rel: Concatenation: || in standard SQL and Oracle; + in SQL Server; CONCAT() function in MySQL/Oracle. Neighbours: CONCAT in Oracle takes two arguments; NULL concatenation behaviour.

qs.stem: Under the standard DML/DDL classification of SQL commands, which of the following is a Data Manipulation Language (DML) statement?
qs.sol:
Concept

SQL groups statements by what they act upon. Data Manipulation Language (DML) operates on the rows stored in tables, whereas Data Definition Language (DDL) changes database structures such as tables and constraints.

Common DML operations insert rows, update row values, and remove rows; structural changes belong to DDL.

Application

DELETE removes rows that satisfy an optional WHERE condition, so it operates on stored table data. Therefore, DELETE is the DML statement among the offered values.

Contrast

ALTER TABLE changes a table definition and is classified as DDL. …
qs.rel: DML operates on rows: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE. Contrast DDL (structure), DCL (privileges), TCL (transactions). Examiners ask which category a command like TRUNCATE or MERGE belongs to.

qs.stem: Which of the following is an optional statement in an SQL query?
qs.sol: A basic SQL query commonly has the form SELECT columns FROM table WHERE condition. The WHERE clause is optional because it is needed only when we want to filter rows. Without WHERE, the query can still return rows from the table. Therefore, option C is correct.
qs.rel: Only SELECT and FROM are mandatory; WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY optional. Execution order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY. WHERE filters rows, HAVING filters groups.

qs.stem: Which of the following category of join returns all records when there is a match in either left or right table?
qs.sol: A Full Outer Join returns all records when there is a match in either the left or right table. It combines both Left and Right Outer Joins, ensuring all rows from both tables are included regardless of matches.
qs.note: Table/figure from the original paper was not captured. Use the explanation to see the correct matching.
qs.rel: Full outer join returns matched plus unmatched rows from both tables (NULL fill). Contrast: left, right, inner. Count: rows = matched + left-only + right-only. Oracle uses FULL OUTER JOIN keyword.

qs.stem: What is self join in Database Management System?

opts.A: In a self join, a table is joined to a number
opts.B: In a self join, a table is joined to itself
opts.C: In a self join, a table is joined with a query
opts.D: In a self join, two databases are joined /

qs.sol: In a self join, a table is joined to itself
qs.rel: Self join joins a table to itself using aliases (employee with manager). Neighbours: needs table aliases, can be inner or outer, equivalent to recursive relationship in ER, hierarchical queries (CONNECT BY).

qs.stem: Which of the following is used for single-line comment in SQL?
qs.sol: In SQL, the double dash '--' is used to create single-line comments within a query. Text following these symbols on the same line is ignored by the database engine.
qs.rel: Comments: -- single line, /* ... */ multi-line (Oracle also REM in SQL*Plus; MySQL also #). Neighbours: statement terminator semicolon, strings in single quotes, keywords case-insensitive.

qs.stem: Identify the SQL wildcard character in Oracle which represents zero, one, or multiple characters?
qs.sol: In Oracle SQL, the percent sign (%) acts as a wildcard for zero, one, or multiple characters. The underscore (_) matches exactly one character instead.
qs.rel: % matches zero or more characters; _ matches exactly one. Example: LIKE 'A%' starts with A; LIKE '_a%' second letter a. Neighbours: ESCAPE, NOT LIKE, wildcard in SQL Server [ ] sets.

qs.stem: Which of the following with respect to views in SQL is FALSE?

opts.A: A view can be derived from the base table or other views.
opts.B: A view is considered as a virtual table.
opts.C: A view exists in the physical form.
opts.D: A view is a single table.

qs.sol:
An ordinary SQL view stores a query definition and presents a virtual table; it is not itself stored as a physical table. A materialized view is a separate concept.

An ordinary view does not itself exist as a physical table.
qs.rel: A view is a stored query (virtual table), not storing data unless materialised. Neighbours: views give security and simplification, simple views updatable, DROP VIEW, WITH CHECK OPTION, materialised view.

qs.stem: Which of the following Oracle SQL statements can be used to select the name of customers who have no address?
qs.sol: In Oracle SQL, standard equality operators do not work with NULL values because comparisons return unknown. You must use the IS NULL operator in your WHERE clause to correctly identify customers who have no address recorded.
qs.rel: NULL needs IS NULL / IS NOT NULL; = NULL is never true (three-valued logic). Neighbours: NVL/COALESCE replace NULL, COUNT(col) ignores NULL, NOT IN with NULL returns nothing.

qs.stem:
Which of the following statement(s) is/are correct regarding Structured Query Language (SQL)?
 I. The datatype FLOAT can hold numbers with decimal points.
 II. The datatype BIGINT occupies 16 bytes.
qs.sol: The datatype FLOAT can hold numbers with decimal points. TRUE
qs.rel: SQL datatypes: FLOAT stores decimals, INT whole numbers, CHAR fixed vs VARCHAR variable, DATE, TIMESTAMP. Neighbours: DECIMAL(p,s) precision/scale, CHAR padding, BLOB/CLOB large objects.

qs.stem:
Which of the following statement is correct for DATEDIFF function in SQL?
I. This function reports difference between the arguments ‘startdate’ and ‘enddate’.
II. In this, ‘datepart’ argument/value can be specified in a variable.
qs.sol: The SQL `DATEDIFF` function returns the difference between `startdate` and `enddate` for a specified date part. In SQL Server, the `datepart` argument is a keyword, not a variable value. Therefore only statement I is correct.
qs.rel: DATEDIFF returns difference between two dates in a specified unit (SQL Server, MySQL days). Neighbours: Oracle uses subtraction and MONTHS_BETWEEN; DATEADD, GETDATE, SYSDATE, NOW.

qs.stem: Which of the following Oracle SQL statements is not correct?

opts.A:
SELECT * FROM Customers 
ORDER BY Country;
opts.B:
SELECT * FROM Customers 
ORDER BY Country DESC;
opts.C:
SELECT * FROM Customers 
ORDER BY Country ASC, DESC CustomerName;
opts.D:
SELECT * FROM Customers 
ORDER BY Country ASC, CustomerName DESC;

qs.sol:
Concept: ORDER BY sorts a query result using a comma-separated list of sort expressions. Each expression may be followed by ASC or DESC; omitting the direction gives ascending order.

Sorting by several expressions uses the later expressions to break ties in earlier ones. SQL syntax is assessed assuming the referenced table and columns exist.

In ORDER BY Country, Country is the sort expression and the omitted direction means ascending country order.

In ORDER BY Country DESC, the direction follows the expression and gives descending country order. …
qs.rel: ORDER BY takes comma-separated expressions, each with ASC/DESC; clause is last in SELECT; GROUP BY and HAVING precede it. Neighbours: invalid syntax like missing commas, aliases usable in ORDER BY, not WHERE.

qs.stem: Which of the following statements is true about TRUNCATE in SQL (Structured Query Language)?

opts.B: TRUNCATE does not remove data from the table.

qs.sol: TRUNCATE removes the rows while preserving the table definition. It is treated as a DDL-style operation, and its page-level deallocation usually makes it faster than DELETE for clearing a table.
qs.rel: TRUNCATE removes all rows quickly, no WHERE, keeps structure, DDL (auto-commit, no rollback in Oracle), resets high-water mark and identity. Contrast: DELETE (WHERE, rollback, triggers fire), DROP.

qs.stem: In Structured Query Language, what is the GROUP BY clause?

opts.A: It groups the table with same name in the database.
opts.B: It groups the rows together that contain the same values in a specific column.
opts.C: It combines data from two tables on specific conditions.
opts.D: It groups the columns together that contain the same values in specific rows.

qs.sol: It groups the rows together that contain the same values in a specific column
qs.rel: GROUP BY groups rows with same values for aggregation; one result row per group. Neighbours: HAVING filters groups, non-aggregated select columns must appear in GROUP BY, ROLLUP/CUBE.

qs.stem: Which of the following mathematical functions in SQL returns the smallest integer greater than, or equal to, the specified numeric expression?
qs.sol:
SQL provides several built-in numeric functions that transform a value in different ways: ROUND adjusts to the nearest value at a given precision, ABS strips the sign to give magnitude, and CEILING and FLOOR round toward a fixed direction rather than to the nearest value.

The question asks for the function that always returns the smallest integer that is greater than or equal to the given expression, the mathematical "ceiling" operation. Testing this against CEILING: CEILING(3.2) evaluates to 4, and CEILING(-3.2) evaluates to -3, in both cases the result is the smallest integer that is still greater than or equal to the input, exactly matching what the question describes. …
qs.rel: CEIL(n) smallest integer >= n; FLOOR(n) largest integer <= n; ROUND rounds to places; TRUNC cuts. Examples: CEIL(4.2)=5, CEIL(-4.2)=-4, FLOOR(-4.2)=-5. MOD, ABS, POWER also single-row.

qs.stem: Which of the following with respect to SQL TRUNCATE statement is true?

opts.A: We may not be able to roll back in case of TRUNCATE in some databases
opts.B: We may roll back truncated data any time
opts.C: After deleting rows, TRUNCATE does not free the space containing table
opts.D: We can use ‘where’ clause with TRUNCATE statement

qs.sol:
TRUNCATE is a DDL operation in many database systems and may commit implicitly, so rollback can be unavailable. Its transaction behavior varies by database.

Rollback availability varies, and some systems commit this operation implicitly.
qs.rel: TRUNCATE is DDL and commits implicitly; so cannot be rolled back, cannot have WHERE, does not fire DELETE triggers. Contrast: DELETE is DML with WHERE and rollback; DROP removes the table.

qs.stem:
Which of the following statement(s) is/are correct regarding single row functions in Structured Query Language?
 Statements:
 I. INSERT() is a numeric function.
 II. ROUND() is a numeric function.
 III. LENGTH() is a character function.
qs.sol: Both II and III
qs.rel: Single-row functions return one value per row and can be nested (character, numeric, date, conversion, general). Contrast: aggregates return one value per group. Examples: UPPER, ROUND, NVL, TO_CHAR.

qs.stem: In SQL, which of the following is correct command for schema evolution, if the RESTRICT option is chosen than the schema is dropped only if schema has no element in it?
qs.sol: With the RESTRICT option, the SQL DROP command drops a schema only when it has no dependent elements. Therefore the command is DROP.
qs.rel: DROP SCHEMA ... RESTRICT drops only if schema empty; CASCADE removes the schema with all its objects. Neighbours: ALTER TABLE DROP COLUMN RESTRICT/CASCADE, DROP TABLE CASCADE CONSTRAINTS.

qs.stem: Which of the following SQL functions is used to evaluate a list of expressions and returns the corresponding result if a value is matched?
qs.sol:
DECODE compares an expression against search values and returns the result paired with the first match.

DECODE maps a matching search value to its paired result.
qs.rel: DECODE(expr, search, result, ..., default) is an Oracle IF-THEN-ELSE; compares for equality. Neighbours: CASE (standard, supports ranges), NVL, NVL2, COALESCE, NULLIF.

qs.stem:
Match the following:

List-1

	

List-2
qs.sol: Classify each command by function. DELETE manipulates data (DML), DROP defines objects (DDL), SAVEPOINT controls transactions (TCL), and GRANT manages permissions (DCL). Thus, the correct sequence matches I-Q, II-P, III-S, IV-R.
qs.rel: Classification: DELETE/INSERT/UPDATE = DML; CREATE/DROP/ALTER/TRUNCATE = DDL; GRANT/REVOKE = DCL; COMMIT/ROLLBACK/SAVEPOINT = TCL; SELECT = DQL. Match-the-column style.

qs.stem:
Consider the following Oracle SQL query: 
SELECT * FROM Products 
WHERE Price BETWEEN 10 AND 20; 
Which of the following is the correct interpretation of this query?

opts.A: Select all products whose price is greater than 10 but less than 20
opts.B: Select all products whose price is greater than or equal to 10 but less than 20
opts.C: Select all products whose price is greater than 10 but less than or equal to 20
opts.D: Select all products whose price is greater than or equal to 10 but less than or equal to 20

qs.sol:
The BETWEEN operator in Oracle SQL (and standard SQL) is always inclusive. This means it includes both the start value and the end value in the results. 

Boundary Values: If a product costs exactly 10 or exactly 20, it will be included in your results.

Order of Values: Always remember that the smaller number must come first. Writing BETWEEN 20 AND 10 would return zero rows because SQL evaluates it strictly from low to high.
qs.rel: BETWEEN a AND b is inclusive of both limits; equivalent to >= a AND <= b. Neighbours: NOT BETWEEN, works on numbers, dates, strings; lower bound must be first; IN checks list membership.

qs.stem: SELECT MAX(result) FROM student WHERE result < (SELECT MAX(result) FROM student);

opts.A: SELECT result FROM student WHERE ROWNUM = 2 ORDER BY result DESC;
opts.B: SELECT TOP 2 result FROM student ORDER BY result DESC;
opts.C: SELECT result FROM student ORDER BY result DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1;
opts.D: SELECT MAX(result) FROM student WHERE result < (SELECT MAX(result) FROM student);

qs.sol: The inner MAX(result) obtains the highest result. The outer query restricts rows to values below that maximum and then takes MAX again, which returns the greatest value below the top result. This is precisely the second-highest distinct result expressed by the fourth SQL statement.
qs.rel: Second-highest value via subquery: MAX of values less than overall MAX. Neighbours: third highest by nested subqueries, LIMIT/OFFSET, ROWNUM, DENSE_RANK, correlated COUNT approach.

qs.stem:
Which of the following statement(s) is/are correct regarding COUNT functions in Structured Query Language of Relational Database Management System?
 I. COUNT(* ) is used to count the number of values in a column.
 II. COUNT() is used to count the number of rows of the query result.
qs.sol:
Concept

SQL aggregate functions reduce a set of input rows to a single result. COUNT(*) counts rows, whereas COUNT(expression) counts rows for which the expression is not NULL.

A function call must also follow valid SQL syntax: empty COUNT() is not a standard COUNT form; an argument such as * or an expression is required.

Application

For Statement I, COUNT(*) is row-oriented. It counts every row that survives the query filters, even when a particular column contains NULL, so it does not mean the count of non-NULL values in one named column.

For Statement II, COUNT() supplies no argument. …
qs.rel: COUNT(*) counts all rows incl. NULLs; COUNT(col) counts non-NULL values; COUNT(DISTINCT col) distinct non-NULL. Neighbours: SUM/AVG ignore NULLs; COUNT returns 0 for empty table, never NULL.

qs.stem: Match the following operators with their definition in data definition language.
qs.sol:
In Data Definition Language (DDL) notation, different symbols are used to represent the structure and occurrence of data elements.

{ } represents iterative/repetitive data, meaning the element can occur multiple times.

( ) represents optional data, meaning the element may or may not be present.

[ , ] represents selection, meaning one choice is selected from the given alternatives.

Therefore, the correct matching is:

1 → iii

2 → i

3 → ii

Hence, the correct answer is: 1-iii, 2-i, 3-ii
qs.note: Table/figure from the original paper was not captured. Use the explanation to see the correct matching.
qs.rel: DDL element definitions: CREATE (new object), ALTER (modify), DROP (delete), TRUNCATE (empty rows), RENAME. Neighbours: constraints defined in DDL, DEFAULT values, schema evolution commands.

qs.stem:
What is the expected output of the given SQL statements on relations borrower and depositor?
“select distinct cust-name from borrower where cust-name not in (select cust-name from depositor)” from relations barrower and depositor ”.

opts.A: All customers who do not have a loan at the bank and do not have an account at the bank.
opts.B: All customers who do not have a loan at the bank, but have an account at the bank.
opts.C: All customers who have a loan at the bank, but do not have an account at the bank.
opts.D: All customers who have a loan at the bank and have an account at the bank.

qs.sol:
The outer borrower query lists loan customers; NOT IN removes those appearing in depositor, leaving loan customers without accounts.

Thus the printed description identifies All customers who have a loan at the bank, but do not have an account at the bank..
qs.rel: NOT IN subquery removes names appearing in subquery set (set difference); DISTINCT removes duplicates. Neighbours: NOT IN fails with NULLs, NOT EXISTS safer, EXCEPT/MINUS equivalent.

qs.stem: Consider the tables PROJECT(Pname,Pnumber,Plocation) and WORKS_ON(ESSN,Pno,Hours). The query to retrieve the project number, project name and number of employees who work on that project is:

opts.A: Select Pnumber,Pname, from PROJECT, WORK_ON where Pnumber=Pno GROUPT BY Pnumber, Pname;
opts.B: Select Pnumber,Pname,COUNT(*) from PROJECT, WORK_ON where Pnumber=Pno;
opts.C: Select Pnumber,Pname,COUNT(*) from PROJECT, WORK_ON GROUPT BY Pnumber, Pname;
opts.D: Select Pnumber,Pname,COUNT(*) from PROJECT, WORK_ON where Pnumber=Pno GROUPT BY Pnumber, Pname;

qs.sol:
The intended query joins projects to work assignments on the project number, groups by project number and name, then counts assignments. The printed keyed option misspells GROUP BY as GROUPT BY and WORKS_ON as WORK_ON, so it is not executable verbatim.

This alone includes join, count and grouping, although the printed SQL has syntax and table-name errors.
qs.rel: Join with GROUP BY: join PROJECT and WORKS_ON on project number, group by project, aggregate SUM/COUNT. Neighbours: HAVING filter, columns in SELECT must be grouped, LEFT JOIN to include projects without work.

qs.stem:
Consider the relations Order(Id,OrderDate,OrderNumber, CustomerId,TotalAmount) and Customer(Id,FirstName,LastName,City,Country,Phone). What will be the output of the following SQL statement:

Select FirstName, LastName,OrderCount= (Select count(O.Id) from Order O where O.CustomerId = C.Id) from Customer C
A

List all customers with all their orders

B

List all customers

C

List all the orders

D

List all customers with their total number of orders
qs.sol:

topics.deep:
- **SQL** = Structured Query Language (originally SEQUEL, IBM; ANSI/ISO standard), declarative database language. Statement categories: **DDL** (CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME - defines structure, auto-commits), **DML** (SELECT/DQL, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE - works on rows), **DCL** (GRANT, REVOKE), **TCL** (COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT, SET TRANSACTION). *INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE are DML; there is no 'INSERT TABLE'.* SQL is not case sensitive for keywords; strings in single quotes; statement ends with semicolon.
- **DDL syntax:** CREATE TABLE emp(id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL, sal DECIMAL(8,2) CHECK(sal>0), dno INT REFERENCES dept(dno), UNIQUE(name)); ALTER TABLE emp ADD age INT; ALTER TABLE emp MODIFY name VARCHAR(50) (Oracle; MySQL also MODIFY, standard ALTER COLUMN); ALTER TABLE emp DROP COLUMN age; DROP TABLE emp (removes data and structure); TRUNCATE TABLE emp (removes all rows, keeps structure, resets storage, cannot use WHERE, typically cannot be rolled back in Oracle as it is DDL, faster than DELETE); DROP SCHEMA s RESTRICT (fails if schema has objects) / CASCADE (drops contents too).
- **DML syntax:** INSERT INTO emp VALUES(1,'A',5000,10); INSERT INTO emp(id,name) VALUES(2,'B'); UPDATE emp SET sal=sal*1.1 WHERE dno=10; DELETE FROM emp WHERE id=1 (may delete zero, one or many rows; without WHERE deletes all rows but keeps table). DELETE is DML (rollbackable), TRUNCATE/DROP are DDL.
- **SELECT clause order:** SELECT [DISTINCT] cols FROM tables [WHERE cond] [GROUP BY cols] [HAVING cond] [ORDER BY cols [ASC|DESC]]. Only SELECT and FROM are mandatory; WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY optional. Logical execution: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY. WHERE filters rows (no aggregates); HAVING filters groups (aggregates allowed). SELECT * = all columns. DISTINCT removes duplicate rows (Oracle also accepts UNIQUE). ORDER BY default ascending.
- **Operators:** comparison =, <>/!=, <, >, <=, >=; BETWEEN a AND b (inclusive both ends); IN (list/subquery); LIKE with wildcards **%** (zero or more chars) and **_** (exactly one char); IS NULL / IS NOT NULL (never = NULL); logical AND, OR, NOT; concatenation **||** (Oracle/standard; MySQL CONCAT(), SQL Server +); comments: -- single line, /* ... */ multi-line; set operators UNION (distinct), UNION ALL, INTERSECT, MINUS (Oracle) / EXCEPT.
- **Aggregate functions:** COUNT(*), COUNT(col) (ignores NULLs), COUNT(DISTINCT col), SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX - all ignore NULLs except COUNT(*). 'Cross product' and 'maximum' are not function names (MAX is). Aggregates collapse many rows to one value; with GROUP BY, one value per group.
- **Single-row functions:** character (UPPER, LOWER, INITCAP, LENGTH, SUBSTR, INSTR, TRIM, LPAD, REPLACE, CONCAT), numeric (ROUND, TRUNC, MOD, POWER, SQRT, ABS, **CEIL = smallest integer >= n**, **FLOOR = largest integer <= n**), date (SYSDATE in Oracle, GETDATE() in SQL Server, NOW() in MySQL, ADD_MONTHS, MONTHS_BETWEEN, DATEDIFF), conversion (TO_CHAR, TO_DATE, TO_NUMBER), general (NVL, NVL2, COALESCE, NULLIF, **DECODE** - IF-THEN-ELSE style, **CASE**). Single-row functions return one value per row and can be nested; they work on columns of any type via conversion.
- **Joins:** INNER JOIN (matching rows only), LEFT OUTER (all left + matched right, else NULL), RIGHT OUTER, FULL OUTER (all rows from both, matched where possible), CROSS JOIN (Cartesian), NATURAL JOIN (on same-named columns), SELF JOIN (table joined to itself using aliases, e.g. employee-manager), equi-join vs non-equi-join. Syntax: SELECT e.name, d.dname FROM emp e JOIN dept d ON e.dno=d.dno.
- **Subqueries:** nested SELECT; uncorrelated runs once, **correlated** references outer row and re-executes per row. Operators IN, NOT IN, ANY, ALL, EXISTS, NOT EXISTS. Second highest: SELECT MAX(r) FROM s WHERE r < (SELECT MAX(r) FROM s). NOT IN returns nothing if the subquery yields a NULL.
- **Views:** CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT ...; virtual table, stores only the query (not data) unless materialised; provides security and simplification; simple views can be updated, complex (joins/aggregates/DISTINCT) generally cannot. DROP VIEW v.
- **Datatypes:** CHAR (fixed), VARCHAR/VARCHAR2, INT/NUMBER, FLOAT (decimals), DECIMAL(p,s), DATE, TIMESTAMP, BLOB, CLOB. Not datatypes: terms like 'real time', 'currency' words unless vendor specific.
- **Constraints:** NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, CHECK, DEFAULT. Indexes: CREATE INDEX. Sequences, synonyms are Oracle objects.
- **Worked example:** SELECT dno, AVG(sal) FROM emp WHERE sal>2000 GROUP BY dno HAVING COUNT(*)>2 ORDER BY dno DESC;  Names with no address: WHERE address IS NULL. Names starting with 'A' and 4 letters: LIKE 'A___'.
- **Typical traps:** = NULL never true; COUNT(col) vs COUNT(*); BETWEEN inclusive; WHERE vs HAVING; DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP; || vs +; DDL auto-commit; SELECT DISTINCT applies to whole row; wildcard % vs _.
- **Likely question angles:** (1) Output of a GROUP BY/HAVING query on a small table. (2) Difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP (rollback, WHERE, speed). (3) Result count of LEFT vs FULL join. (4) LIKE pattern matching a given set of strings. (5) What does COUNT(col) return with NULLs. (6) Which clause comes after GROUP BY. (7) Output of NVL / COALESCE / DECODE. (8) Which SQL command grants privileges. (9) Updatable views. (10) Output of a set operator query (UNION vs UNION ALL). (11) ROUND vs TRUNC vs CEIL.

topics.title: 5. Functional Dependencies & Normalisation
topics.theory:
- **FD X → Y:** X (left side = **determinant**) determines Y (right side = **dependent**). **Armstrong's axioms:** Reflexivity, Augmentation, Transitivity; derived: **Union** (α→β, α→γ ⇒ α→βγ), **Decomposition** (α→βγ ⇒ α→β and α→γ), **Pseudo-transitivity** (α→β, γβ→δ ⇒ αγ→δ).
- **Prime attribute** = part of some candidate key; non-prime = not part of any. R(A,B,C,D) with candidate keys AB and C → prime = A, B, C.
- **Candidate keys:** compute attribute closure X⁺; key = minimal set with X⁺ = all attributes. Attributes never on any RHS must be in every key.
- **1NF:** all attribute values **atomic** (no repeating groups / relations within relations). **2NF:** 1NF + **no partial dependency** (every non-prime attribute fully dependent on the key). **3NF:** 2NF + **no transitive dependency** of non-key attribute on key (non-trivial FD X→A: X is a super key or A is prime). **BCNF:** every determinant is a super key. 4NF removes multivalued dependencies; 5NF join dependencies. **2NF ⇒ 1NF; BCNF ⇒ 3NF ⇒ 2NF ⇒ 1NF.**
- Single-key relation Employee(SSN, Name) with SSN key is in BCNF. **Denormalisation** = deliberately increasing redundancy to improve read performance.

qs.stem: If a relation schema is in 2NF, then it is definitely in:
qs.sol: Database normalization follows a hierarchical structure where each higher normal form builds upon the previous one. To achieve Second Normal Form (2NF), a relation must first satisfy all conditions of First Normal Form (1NF). Consequently, any schema in 2NF is inherently guaranteed to be in 1NF as well.
qs.rel: Normal-form hierarchy: BCNF implies 3NF implies 2NF implies 1NF. Neighbours: 2NF removes partial dependency, 3NF transitive, BCNF every determinant a super key; reverse implications do not hold.

qs.stem: Third normal form (3NF) is dependent on which of the following concepts?
qs.sol:
Third normal form addresses transitive dependencies of non-key attributes on a key.

Removing those dependencies is the usual route from 2NF to 3NF.
qs.rel: 3NF is based on transitive dependency (non-prime depends on non-key via another non-prime). Contrast: 2NF - full functional dependency (no partial), BCNF - determinant must be super key.

qs.stem: All candidate keys other than primary keys are known as ______.
qs.sol: Modified from the official paper: The official paper cancelled the item. In relational database terminology, candidate keys that were not chosen as the primary key are alternate keys.
qs.rel: Alternate keys = candidate keys not chosen as primary key (secondary keys). Neighbours: super key, composite key, surrogate key, foreign key; a relation may have several candidate keys but one primary.

qs.stem: If for a relation schema R, the domains of all attributes of R are atomic, then R is said to be in which normal form?
qs.sol:
Atomic attribute domains are the defining condition for first normal form.

Thus the printed description identifies First normal form.
qs.rel: 1NF requires atomic domains (no repeating groups or relations within relations). Neighbours: composite and multivalued attributes violate 1NF, 2NF needs full dependence, BCNF stronger than 3NF.

qs.stem: The left-hand side and the right-hand sides of a functional dependency are sometimes called _____ and _____ respectively.
qs.sol: determinant; dependent
qs.rel: In an FD X -> Y, left side is determinant, right side dependent. Neighbours: trivial FD, Armstrong's axioms, closure X+, candidate key determines all attributes.

qs.stem: If AB and C are the candidate keys in a relation schema R(A,B,C,D), then what are the prime attributes?
qs.sol: Prime attributes are defined as any attribute that is part of at least one candidate key. Since the candidate keys are AB and C, the attributes A, B, and C constitute the set of prime attributes.
qs.rel: Prime attributes belong to some candidate key; with keys AB and C in R(A,B,C,D) prime = A,B,C, non-prime = D. Neighbours: 2NF concerns non-prime attributes; 3NF allows prime on right side.

qs.stem: If a relation x has more than one key, then each of the keys can be called as:
qs.sol:
Each minimal key capable of uniquely identifying a tuple is a candidate key.

One candidate is selected as the primary key.
qs.rel: Relation with multiple keys: each is a candidate key; one chosen primary, rest alternate. Neighbours: super key not minimal, number of candidate keys via closure, key attributes prime.

qs.stem: Consider an Employee(SSN, Name) relation with atomic values, SSN as its candidate key, and no nontrivial functional dependencies with an empty determinant. What is the highest normal form satisfied?
qs.sol: Modified from the official paper: the printed Employee (SSN, Name) question gives neither atomicity nor a candidate key or functional dependencies, so its highest normal form cannot be determined from the printed stem alone. Here the added assumptions make SSN a candidate key, exclude empty-determinant nontrivial dependencies, and specify atomic values. Every possible nontrivial determinant is then a superkey, so the relation satisfies BCNF.
qs.rel: Two-attribute relation with atomic values and key SSN has no partial or transitive dependency, so BCNF. Neighbours: relation with only two attributes is always BCNF; 3NF but not BCNF needs overlapping composite keys.

qs.stem: Which of the following normal form of normalization in relational model, disallows relations within relations or relations as attribute values within tuples?
qs.sol: First Normal Form requires atomic attribute values, so it disallows relations within relations or relation-valued attributes inside tuples.
qs.rel: 1NF disallows relations within relations / multivalued and composite attributes (nested relations). Neighbours: unnormalised form, repeating groups, atomic values, 4NF handles multivalued dependency.

qs.stem: What is Denormalization in Relational Database Management System?

opts.A: Denormalization is the process of increasing redundancy to improve performance.
opts.B: Denormalization is used to decrease redundancy in database.
opts.C: Denormalization is used to decrease the dependence on normal forms.
opts.D: Denormalization is used to develop a new schema in database.

qs.sol:
Concept: Normalization organizes a relational schema to eliminate redundant data and keep every fact stored in exactly one place, which protects data integrity but forces read queries to join many small tables together. Denormalization is the deliberate reverse of that trade-off: it reintroduces controlled redundancy — duplicating columns, merging related tables, or precomputing derived values — so that read-heavy queries can retrieve data with fewer joins, at the cost of some update overhead and storage.

Application: For this question, denormalization is defined precisely as the process of increasing redundancy in a schema in order to improve (read) performance. …
qs.rel: Denormalization adds redundancy deliberately to speed queries (fewer joins), used in warehouses; costs anomalies and storage. Contrast: normalisation reduces redundancy; star schema denormalised.

qs.stem:
Which of the following statement(s) is/are correct regarding a relation in second normal form?

I. It is in first normal form

II. Every non-key attribute is fully and functionally independent on the primary key
qs.sol:
Concept: Functional dependence X → Y means that equal X values always give equal Y values. Full dependence means no proper subset of X determines Y.

A relation is in second normal form (2NF) when it is in first normal form (1NF) and every non-prime attribute is fully dependent on every candidate key. First normal form requires atomic values in each field.

Application: Consider Enrolment(StudentID, CourseID, Grade), with (StudentID, CourseID) as its only candidate key and Grade as its only non-prime attribute. Assume the intended dependencies require the complete pair. …
qs.rel: 2NF = 1NF + no partial dependency of non-prime attributes on part of a candidate key. Neighbours: relation with single-attribute key automatically 2NF; partial dependency needs composite key; 3NF adds no transitive.

Armstrong's Axioms define functional dependencies in database normalization. Decomposition (I) matches P, splitting βγ into separate dependencies.

Union (II) matches R, combining α → β and α → γ into a single dependency. Pseudotransitivity (III) matches Q, chaining dependencies via intermediate attributes.

Augmentation (IV) matches S, adding attributes to both sides of a dependency. The correct sequence is I-P, II-R, III-Q, IV-S.
